newsitem.title: MONTSERRAT: Prince Andrew gets taste of Montserrat volcano.
newsitem.headline: Prince Andrew gets taste of Montserrat volcano.

text.p: After days of relative quiet, Montserrat's rumbling volcano let loose a cloud of ash on Wednesday, showering Britain's Prince Andrew as he toured the island's abandoned capital.

The ash cloud darkened the sky and rolled down the flank of the Soufriere Hills volcano as the Duke of York walked the rubble-strewn streets of Plymouth, finally reaching the royal party. His aides scrambled for surgical masks and the prince put one on as muddy volcanic ash rained from the sky, spattering Andrew's tropical combat fatigues and green beret.
Andrew, a lieutenant-commander in the Royal Navy, arrived on Tuesday for a two-day tour of this British Caribbean colony plagued for nearly 19 months by the cantankerous volcano.

Montserrat officials hoped his visit would aid their bid for more British aid to construct new housing in the north of the island, considered the safe zone. The British government last August pledged $39 million (25 million pounds) in aid.

The volcanic activity has forced three evacuations of the island's south end. The last, 10 months ago, left the capital largely abandoned and crammed thousands of people into homes and public shelters in the north.

Andrew drove past dozens of boarded-up shops and homes in the once-bustling capital, walked through ash-clogged streets and clambered into Fort Ghaut, once the main drainage channel in Plymouth and now choked with 10 feet (3 metres) of volcanic debris.

He visited Government House, a turn-of-the-century seaside mansion on which a $1.5 million (one million pound) renovation was completed just before the volcano burst to life in July 1995. The historic terraced home of the island's governor was boarded up and abandoned when the capital was evacuated.
Then, as he chatted with dock workers at the town pier, Andrew got a taste of what islanders have endured for 19 months as the ash cloud swept over the port.
"I think it's sad to see that Plymouth is devastated the way it is," the prince said. "But this is the key. If they can keep the port open ... then Montserrat has a chance."

Andrew later sat in a makeshift classroom where schoolchildren described the hardships of the volcano. He chatted with residents of a shelter and conferred the title of "Royal" on the Montserrat Defence Force for its work during the crisis.
Vulcanologists said the rumbling mountain twice belched small "pyroclastic" flows of rock and hot gases on Wednesday, creating the ash clouds that enveloped the prince's party.

"That's the biggest flow we've had in about four days," seismologist Rod Stewart said, adding that they were small flows compared to some seen on the island, the largest of which have roared down at 60 mph (100 kph) to the sea.
